final.title: Why stopping rules miss the real workflow decision
final.body:
Stopping rules sound tidy until you hit the real workflow. In a small business, the issue is usually not the first rule. It is the exception: the invoice that sits outside the normal range, the customer record that is incomplete, the lead that needs a human eye. A simple if-then rule can stop work, but it can also stop the wrong work or let the wrong thing through.

So the practical question is this: in your repeated workflow, what judgment calls do you keep making by hand that a fixed rule would miss? If the answer is “almost none,” AI probably is not worth the effort. If the answer is “quite a few,” map the exceptions on one page. Mark which ones should always go to a person, which ones can be checked automatically, and which ones must never be auto-approved.

That boundary matters most when money is involved. Bareni’s accounts-payable demo showed amount-based human-only approval, duplicate-invoice blocking, and refusal of agent approval or payment attempts, using entirely synthetic data. The blocked payment was a manual simulation, not a real transfer. Human approval stays mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

If your work already lives in digital documents and SaaS tools, the next step is simple: audit one recurring workflow for the exceptions that a stopping rule would miss. The cost of a wrong rule is usually more obvious after the fact.

final.title: Why stopping rules are not enough in small-business workflows
final.body:
Stopping rules sound neat until you meet the real workflow. In a small business, the problem is usually not the first rule. It is the exception: the invoice that is over the usual amount, the customer record that is incomplete, the lead that looks promising but still needs a human eye. A simple if-then rule can stop work, but it can also stop the wrong work or let the wrong thing through. That is why bounded automation should start with the exception path, not the happy path.

The practical question is simple: in your repeated workflow, what judgment calls keep happening by hand that a fixed rule would miss? If the answer is almost none, AI probably is not worth the trouble. If the answer is several, map those exceptions on one page. Mark which ones are safe to route to a person, which ones can be checked automatically, and which ones must stay under human approval.

That boundary matters most where money is involved. Bareni’s approved AP demo shows amount-based human-only approval and refusal of agent payment attempts, using entirely synthetic data and a manual simulated trigger. The point is not to let software quietly decide the risky bit. Less glamorous, more useful.

If your workflow lives in digital documents and SaaS tools, and it repeats often enough to have a measurable outcome, the next step is simple: audit one workflow for the exceptions that stopping rules miss. Then decide whether it is a manual job, a hiring job, or a bounded automation job.
